questions.question: Which situation calls for a two-sample (independent) t-test?
options: The same 12 patients measured before and after a drug
Reaction times of 40 men versus 35 women
One sample compared with a known value
questions.explanation: Two separate groups of different people are independent samples. Before/after on the same people is paired, and one sample against a value is a one-sample test.

questions.question: H₀ for a two-sample t-test (two-tailed) is usually...
questions.explanation: H₀ says the population means are equal. It concerns parameters, not sample means.

questions.question: Group A (n = 30, mean 74, SD 8) and Group B (n = 30, mean 79, SD 7). What is the t statistic?
For the same data (df ≈ 57, critical value 2.002), what is the decision at α = 0.05?
options: Fail to reject, since the difference is small
Reject only with a one-tailed test
questions.explanation: |t| = 2.576 exceeds the critical value, so p ≈ 0.013 < 0.05. Reject H₀.

questions.question: Why is Welch's t-test the safer default?
options: It always gives a smaller p-value
It does not assume equal population variances and keeps the false-alarm rate near α
questions.explanation: When variances and sample sizes differ, the pooled test can have a false-alarm rate far above 5% (26% in the lesson's example), while Welch stays near 5%.

questions.question: A 95% CI for μ₁ − μ₂ is (−8.9, −1.1). What does this tell you?
options: Group 1's mean is lower, by roughly 1 to 9 units
questions.explanation: The interval excludes 0, so the difference is significant at 5%. It is entirely negative, so group 1 is lower, and the interval shows how big the gap plausibly is.
